questions.prompt: Why did many medieval European monarchs depend on local nobles?
choices: Nobles controlled land, so kings had no recognized legal claim to rule over their own kingdoms
Nobles were appointed through examinations that kings were required to accept
Nobles controlled land, armed men, and local justice that kings could not run directly
Nobles paid all royal taxes, so kings never needed revenue of their own
questions.explanation: Limited revenue and slow communication made kings rely on lords who held land and followers.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Nobles held land, but kings still claimed authority; the issue was practical control.
European nobility was largely hereditary, not selected by examination.
Limited revenue and slow communication made kings rely on lords who held land and followers.
Kings collected their own revenues, though limited ones; that limit is part of the explanation.
questions.distinguisher: The problem was practical capacity, not legal title.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Giovanni Boccaccio, Florentine writer, introduction to The Decameron, completed c. 1353, describing Florence and its countryside during the plague of 1348
stimulusBlocks.citation: The Decameron of Giovanni Boccaccio, trans. John Payne (London: Villon Society, 1886), First Day, introduction. Project Gutenberg eBook #23700.
stimulusBlocks.note: Husbandmen are farmers. Payne's 1886 English imitates older usage.
stimulusBlocks.text:
By reason whereof there remained unto those (and the number of them, both males and females, was incalculable) who fell sick, none other succour than that which they owed either to the charity of friends (and of these there were few) or the greed of servants, who tended them, allured by high and extravagant wage . . . .

throughout the scattered villages and in the fields, the poor and miserable husbandmen and their families, without succour of physician or aid of servitor, died, not like men, but well nigh like beasts, by the ways or in their tillages or about the houses, indifferently by day and night. . . . the oxen, the asses, the sheep, the goats, the swine, the fowls, nay, the very dogs, so faithful to mankind, being driven forth of their own houses, went straying at their pleasure about the fields, where the very corn was abandoned, without being cut, much less gathered in

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.6 learning objectives and historical developments

questions.prompt: According to Boccaccio, the authority of the laws collapsed in Florence because
choices: the Church had excommunicated the city's rulers
the officials who enforced the laws had abandoned the city for the countryside
the city's merchants had overthrown the government
the officials who enforced the laws were dead, sick, or without assistants
questions.explanation: He writes that the ministers of the law were dead, sick, or left without followers, so no one could enforce it.
choiceExplanations: No excommunication appears in the passage.
Flight is described for ordinary people, not given as the reason officials failed.
Boccaccio describes no political revolt.
He writes that the ministers of the law were dead, sick, or left without followers, so no one could enforce it.
questions.distinguisher: Boccaccio says many people fled, but he blames the collapse of law on officials being dead, sick, or without followers.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Giovanni Boccaccio, Florentine writer, introduction to The Decameron, completed c. 1353, describing Florence during the plague of 1348
stimulusBlocks.citation: The Decameron of Giovanni Boccaccio, trans. John Payne (London: Villon Society, 1886), First Day, introduction. Project Gutenberg eBook #23700.
stimulusBlocks.note: Bracketed words are the translator's. Payne's 1886 English imitates older usage; “recking of nought” means caring about nothing.
stimulusBlocks.text:
In this sore affliction and misery of our city, the reverend authority of the laws, both human and divine, was all in a manner dissolved and fallen into decay, for [lack of] the ministers and executors thereof, who, like other men, were all either dead or sick or else left so destitute of followers that they were unable to exercise any office, wherefore every one had license to do whatsoever pleased him. . . .

Some were of a more barbarous, though, peradventure, a surer way of thinking, avouching that there was no remedy against pestilences better than--no, nor any so good as--to flee before them; wherefore, moved by this reasoning and recking of nought but themselves, very many, both men and women, abandoned their own city, their own houses and homes, their kinsfolk and possessions, and sought the country seats of others, or, at the least, their own . . . .

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a long-term effect of the crisis Boccaccio describes in parts of western Europe?
choices: Labor shortages that led lords to free all serfs voluntarily
Labor shortages that strengthened the bargaining power of surviving workers
The immediate end of serfdom in every European kingdom
The rapid growth of European population in the following decades
questions.explanation: So many deaths left fewer workers, who in some regions could demand higher wages and better terms.
choiceExplanations: Lords often resisted change, and laws tried to limit wages and mobility.
So many deaths left fewer workers, who in some regions could demand higher wages and better terms.
Serfdom declined unevenly and lasted for centuries in eastern Europe.
The plague sharply reduced population; recovery took generations.
questions.distinguisher: Labor shortages were real, but lords and governments often tried to hold down wages and keep peasants bound.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, which of the following best describes political authority in much of western Europe?
choices: Authority was divided between kings and landholding nobles
Authority was held mainly by elected town councils
Authority was divided between kings and Mongol governors
Authority was centralized in salaried officials chosen by examination
questions.explanation: Kings depended on nobles who held land, collected rents, held courts, and kept armed followers.
choiceExplanations: Kings depended on nobles who held land, collected rents, held courts, and kept armed followers.
Towns gained some rights, but nobles controlled most local authority.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 1.6, KC-3.2.I.B.ii and KC-3.3.III.C: Europe was politically fragmented, with decentralized monarchies, feudalism, and the manorial system, and depended on free and coerced labor including serfdom
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing how historians describe lordship and labor in Europe, c. 1200–1450
stimulusBlocks.text:
In much of western Europe, kings depended on nobles who held land in return for loyalty and military service. These lords collected rents and labor from the peasants on their estates, held courts, and kept armed followers. A king who wanted to raise an army or a tax often had to bargain with them.

On many manors, serfs were bound to the land and owed their lord days of labor each week, along with fees for using his mill or for marrying. Yet the system was never uniform. Free peasants rented land for money, towns won charters that limited lords' control, and after the plague of 1348 surviving laborers in some regions demanded higher wages.

questions.prompt: Which of the following details from the passage best supports the claim that the manorial system was not uniform?
choices: Free peasants rented land for money
Kings had to bargain with nobles to raise armies
Serfs owed their lords days of labor each week
Lords held courts and kept armed followers
questions.explanation: Free peasants paying rent show that not everyone was a serf.
choiceExplanations: Free peasants paying rent show that not everyone was a serf.
Bargaining concerns kings and nobles, not variation among peasants.
Labor dues show the typical pattern, not variation.
Courts and armed followers describe lords' power, not variation in the system.
questions.distinguisher: Labor dues describe how manors usually worked; the claim needs an exception to the pattern.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which of the following contributed to the work of scholars such as Thomas Aquinas?
choices: Translations of Aristotle made by Mongol officials in Baghdad
Translations of Aristotle that reached Latin readers largely through Arabic
Printed books produced on Gutenberg's press
Greek texts brought by scholars fleeing the fall of Constantinople
questions.explanation: The passage says Aristotle reached Latin readers largely through translations from Arabic.
choiceExplanations: Mongol officials did not produce these translations; Iberian centers such as Toledo did.
The passage says Aristotle reached Latin readers largely through translations from Arabic.
Gutenberg's press came about two centuries after Aquinas.
Constantinople fell in 1453, long after Aquinas.
questions.distinguisher: Byzantine scholars did bring Greek texts west, but mostly after 1453, long after Aquinas died in 1274.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 1.6, KC-3.1.III.D.v: Christianity, Judaism, Islam, and their core beliefs and practices continued to shape societies in Europe
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing how historians describe the Church and learning in Europe, c. 1200–1450
stimulusBlocks.text:
The Roman Catholic Church was the largest landowner in western Europe and the main sponsor of education. Universities such as those at Paris and Oxford grew out of church schools in the 1100s and 1200s. There, scholars such as Thomas Aquinas used the logic of Aristotle, whose works had reached Latin readers largely through translations from Arabic, to explain Christian teaching.

The Church's authority did not go unchallenged. Popes and kings argued over who could appoint bishops and tax clergy, and Jewish communities, which contributed to medicine and trade, faced expulsions from England in 1290 and from France in 1306.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would most directly support the claim in the second paragraph?
choices: Evidence that universities taught theology alongside law and medicine
Evidence that popes supported crusades in the eastern Mediterranean
Evidence that most European peasants attended church regularly
Evidence that kings and popes disputed control over appointing bishops
questions.explanation: Disputes over appointing bishops show rulers contesting Church authority, which is the claim.
choiceExplanations: University teaching shows the Church's role in education, not opposition to it.
Supporting crusades demonstrates papal power rather than a challenge to it.
Church attendance shows influence, not challenges to it.
Disputes over appointing bishops show rulers contesting Church authority, which is the claim.
questions.distinguisher: Crusades show papal influence; the claim is that the Church's authority was challenged.

questions.prompt: Which development in the passage most directly made possible the growth of towns?
choices: Rising food output that could support people who did not farm
A single law code issued by the Church for all of Europe
A fall in population that raised the value of labor

choiceExplanations: Better plows, horse collars, and the three-field system produced surplus food, which freed people to work in towns as merchants and artisans.
The passage describes no common law code, and the Church did not issue one.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 1.6 key concept: Europe's agricultural, commercial, and educational growth, c. 1200–1450
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing growth and authority in Western Europe, c. 1200–1450
stimulusBlocks.text:
By 1200, a growing population and better farming methods, including heavier plows, horse collars, and the three-field system, had increased food output in Western Europe. Towns expanded, and merchants and artisans formed guilds to regulate their trades. Italian cities such as Venice and Genoa used their ships to carry goods between the Mediterranean and Europe's interior, and fairs in Champagne drew merchants from many regions.

The Catholic Church shaped learning. Universities in Bologna, Paris, and Oxford trained clergy and lawyers, and scholars studied works of Aristotle that had been preserved and translated through the Islamic world. Historians add that European kings were weaker than the rulers of China or the great Islamic states, because power was divided among kings, nobles, towns, and the Church.

questions.prompt: The study of Aristotle at European universities most directly reflects the influence of
choices: the spread of printing presses that made books cheap across Europe
Byzantine scholars who brought Greek texts to Italy after 1453
scholarship preserved and translated through the Islamic world
the revival of Roman law studied at Bologna
questions.explanation: The passage says Aristotle's works were preserved and translated through the Islamic world before European scholars studied them.
choiceExplanations: Movable-type printing in Europe began in the 1450s, after the period of the passage.
Greek scholars fleeing Constantinople came after 1453, long after universities began studying Aristotle.
The passage says Aristotle's works were preserved and translated through the Islamic world before European scholars studied them.
Bologna revived Roman law, but the passage links Aristotle's works to translation through the Islamic world.
questions.distinguisher: Printing helped spread Renaissance and Reformation ideas, but the transfer of Aristotle's texts came centuries earlier through Islamic scholars.

stimulusBlocks.text:
By 1200, a growing population and better farming methods, including heavier plows, horse collars, and the three-field system, had increased food output in Western Europe. Towns expanded, and merchants and artisans formed guilds to regulate their trades. Italian cities such as Venice and Genoa used their ships to carry goods between the Mediterranean and Europe's interior, and fairs in Champagne drew merchants from many regions.

The Catholic Church shaped learning. Universities in Bologna, Paris, and Oxford trained clergy and lawyers, and scholars studied works of Aristotle that had been preserved and translated through the Islamic world. Historians add that European kings were weaker than the rulers of China or the great Islamic states, because power was divided among kings, nobles, towns, and the Church.
